care: On Christian Doctrine is a guide to reading and teaching the Bible, written by a Christian bishop for Christian teachers. The lesson presents Augustine’s aims and rules as his own, and draws out the parts about signs, language and speaking that any reader can use.

young.html: Augustine was a bishop in North Africa who had once been a teacher of public speaking. He wrote a book for people who read the Bible and teach it to others. It is called On Christian Doctrine; “doctrine” here means teaching.

Augustine noticed that everything we learn comes to us through signs. A sign is something that makes you think of something else. Some signs happen by themselves: when you see smoke, you think of fire, even though nobody sent the smoke as a message. Augustine called these natural signs. Other signs are given on purpose, like words, a nod or a wave. He called these conventional signs, because people agree on what they mean.

young.name: gb-signs
young.cap: Is it a plain thing, a natural sign or a given sign? Choose, then tap Next example.

young.html: A sign hunt. Walk around your home or street and find five natural signs (wet pavement means it rained; a wagging tail means a happy dog) and five given signs (a stop sign, a label, a clock face, a smile meant for you). Make two lists. Which list was easier? Can you find something that could be both?

full.html: Augustine (AD 354–430) began On Christian Doctrine (Latin De doctrina christiana) soon after he became bishop of Hippo, around AD 396. He stopped partway through the third book and came back to it about thirty years later, in 426–427, when he finished Book III and added Book IV. His purpose was practical: to teach Christian readers how to understand the Bible, and preachers how to explain it to others. Along the way he wrote one of the first careful accounts of how signs and language work.

full.text: All instruction is either about things or about signs; but things are learnt by means of signs. I now use the word “thing” in a strict sense, to signify that which is never employed as a sign of anything else: for example, wood, stone, cattle, and other things of that kind.
full.author: Augustine
full.work: On Christian Doctrine, Book I, chapter 2
full.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

full.html: Book I is about things. Augustine divides them into things to be enjoyed, loved for their own sake, and things to be used, loved for the sake of something else (in Latin, frui and uti). In his view only God is to be enjoyed in the full sense, and everything else rightly loved in relation to God. The whole aim of Scripture, he says, is love of God and of neighbor: whoever thinks he understands the Bible but does not build up that double love has not yet understood it.

full.text: For a sign is a thing which, over and above the impression it makes on the senses, causes something else to come into the mind as a consequence of itself: as when we see a footprint, we conclude that an animal whose footprint this is has passed by; and when we see smoke, we know that there is fire beneath.
full.author: Augustine
full.work: On Christian Doctrine, Book II, chapter 1
full.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

full.html: Natural signs point to something without anyone intending them to: smoke, a footprint, an angry face. Conventional (given) signs are used on purpose to pass a thought from one mind to another: words above all, and also nods, gestures, flags and trumpet calls. Written letters are signs of spoken words, so writing is a sign of a sign.

full.name: gb-signs
full.cap: Sort Augustine’s examples, and some of ours, into things, natural signs and conventional signs.

full.text: Hard passages and the tools to read them

full.html: Book II asks why Scripture is sometimes hard to understand. Signs can be unknown (you do not know the word or the thing it names) or ambiguous (they could mean more than one thing). For unknown signs, Augustine says, learn the languages, Hebrew and Greek, and compare translations; learn history, natural history, numbers and music. He argues that a Christian should take whatever is true and useful in pagan learning, as the Israelites carried gold and silver out of Egypt, and he puts the principle simply:

full.text: Let every good and true Christian understand that wherever truth may be found, it belongs to his Master.
full.author: Augustine
full.work: On Christian Doctrine, Book II, chapter 18
full.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

full.html: Book III takes up ambiguous signs, and especially the question of when to read words literally and when figuratively. One of his rules: a passage that, read literally, would seem to recommend something contrary to love or to good morals should be read as figurative. He also discusses the seven rules of interpretation of an earlier African writer, Tyconius.

full.text: Book IV: to teach, to delight, to persuade

full.html: The former professor of rhetoric now writes about speaking. He borrows Cicero’s three aims of the speaker.

full.text: Accordingly a great orator has truly said that “an eloquent man must speak so as to teach, to delight, and to persuade.” Then he adds: “To teach is a necessity, to delight is a beauty, to persuade is a triumph.”
full.author: Augustine
full.work: On Christian Doctrine, Book IV, chapter 12
full.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

full.html: Teaching comes first: a speaker who is not understood, Augustine says, has not yet said anything to his hearer. He matches Cicero’s three styles to the three aims: the subdued (plain) style for teaching, the temperate (middle) style for delighting, and the majestic (grand) style for moving people to act. A good speaker mixes them, and his life must match his words, or his words will carry little weight.

Thinking Augustine rejects rhetoric because it is pagan. He says rhetoric is a tool that can serve truth or falsehood, so those who teach truth should not leave it to those who teach lies. What he warns against is eloquence without wisdom: a beautiful speech that says nothing true.

items: Education: for the whole Middle Ages this book was a charter for Christian learning, justifying the study of grammar, rhetoric, history and the sciences.
The study of signs: Augustine’s definition of a sign and his split between natural and conventional signs are still discussed by philosophers of language.
Preaching and speaking: Book IV is often called the first Christian handbook of rhetoric, and teachers of speech still use its three aims.

deep.text: Context: a teacher of speech becomes a bishop

deep.html: Augustine had spent his early career teaching young men to speak persuasively in court and in public. As a bishop he preached often to ordinary people in a busy port city. This book brings the two lives together. It also reflects a real question in the Church of his time: should Christians study the pagan classics, Virgil and Cicero, or leave them alone? Augustine’s answer, keep what is true and useful, shaped Christian schools for a thousand years.

items: Is everything we learn really learned through signs? What about learning to ride a bike?
Can a beautiful speech be bad? Can a plain one be great?
How should we decide whether words are meant literally or as a figure of speech?
Should a speaker try to delight and persuade, or only to teach?

deep.html: Thomas Aquinas, in the next era, discusses the literal and spiritual senses of Scripture, building on Augustine. Erasmus, in the Renaissance, renewed the call to read Scripture in Hebrew and Greek. Much later, Locke’s Essay Concerning Human Understanding, on this ladder, opened a new study of words as signs of ideas.

questions: What signs have you used today without words? (A nod, a wave, a thumbs-up.)
Augustine says a speaker who is not understood has said nothing. Have you ever explained something and not been understood? What did you change?
Which matters most in a speech: teaching, delighting, or persuading? Why?
“Wherever truth may be found, it belongs to his Master.” Why might Augustine want Christians to study books by people who did not share their faith?
Can you think of a sentence that means something different when read literally and when read as a figure of speech?
